I have a really weird relationship with this.

I resent being used purely for my utility. I had a friend whom I never used to see unless she needed a ride to the grocery store, or to use a landline phone for a job interview, or because she was stranded somewhere. It wasn't anywhere close to equal exchange either. I never really got anything back from her, she just took and took and took.

In the middle, I've had I suppose "Symbiotic" associations with people. I didn't necessarily LIKE them, I didn't spend my free time with them or look forward to the next time I'd see them (but neither did I dread them). But our utilitarian association went both ways. They needed a particular ancient computer part? Sure, I've got one of those, I can bail them out. Couple months later, they upgrade somebody's network hardware? Sweet, I've got a 24 port managed switch for my home network now! It flowed both ways, and neither was taking advantage of the other.

And then, I forget how the exact conversation went, but one of my friends once referred to me as "The Useful One" because of my penchant for obsessive levels of preparedness. Whenever we go camping, I've got virtually everything we need for the whole trip. When the power was knocked out for the whole city, I had the generator to charge devices and candles to play boardgames by. Somebody's $20 short? I've got their back. need me to use the spare key and clear your browser history before your wife gets home? I'm on it secret agent style. And I take a lot of pride in that observation. I really enjoy being 'the useful one' as he put it. And I don't feel ill used when I can provide like that for a friend. Especially when It's a friend I know has my back right back. When I know I can text them when I'm sick as death and ask them to drop off some nyquil on their way home from work, or to grab me some dinner before they come over to game.

In a lot of ways how much value we add to people's lives is uncomfortably important. It's not something people like to dwell on or discuss. I don't think it necessarily needs to be symmetrical, but it shouldn't be unidirectional either.

I don't know you, so maybe you already know this and don't care but I think you are literally a high functioning psychopath.

I guess society gives psychopathy a negative connotation and from what I have read your argument is that psychopathy is ok.

Real human relationships are NOT based on some sort of "I get X and you get Y" type formula. That is a business relationship and most people purposely separate personal and business relationships explicitly. When personal and business is mixed people still use contracts to try to separate what parts of their lives are business and what parts are friendships.

Regular people pick friends first and then if they happen to have a truck they might ask the person to help them with something and then be OVERLY generous when that sort of favor is given. The key point is that this friendship is NOT based on the truck. The friendship would exist without the truck. The truck is something that would be "dumb" to not utilize. i.e. why go rent a truck when your friend has one.

This is absolutely not the same as having a friend BECAUSE he has a truck and the friendship would be over if he did not have a truck. That is a business relationship and should be treated as such.

I don't disagree that friendships are based on "exchange" of value but it is not about you provide X for your friend and they provide Y and when your friend can't provide Y, its over. At any given time those may not balance but there is never an expectation that they will. Sort of like insurance. You are abusing this aspect - the fact that friendships are rarely 100% balanced at a given time. You take advantage of when the balance is in your favor and leave when it needs to tip the other way.

edit The reason I believe you are a psychopath is because you are fully aware of what you are doing and feel no negative emotions. You SHOULD feel bad for what you are doing. Most people at least feel bad when the use people the way you describe, even if they do it anyway.

I mean, since people do get upset about this I try to hide it because I don't want to hurt someone's feelings (or lose the perk), but why does it bother people? It's nice to be useful. Occasionally there are people I really like and have a relationship like you described, but that's a very rare thing.

I've taken the most widely used self-report test for psychopathy (used a lot a in studies as it correlates well to the diagnosis) and I am rather high on that scale. I didn't really think of this behavior as a manifestation of that though. I don't generally like the term because people act like you're some kind of reptile. I have feelings, I love people, and I do have empathy. I'm just fairly ruthless, rational, thrill-seeking, risk-taking, and fairly low empathy.

The reason why you don't or can't feel bad is a symptom of psychopathy. You should be able to put yourself in the other persons shoes. What they think they have is someone who like them for the person that they are and that they happen to have some useful skills or possessions that they can use to show that they like you for the person you are. The problem is it is fake on your side. This thought on their side also means they don't think you will abandon them if they lose their "truck" - because you don't like them for the "truck", you like them for their personality.

You mistakenly believe that these people are willing to trade a temporary fake friendship for favors. The truth is a fake friendship is not the same as a real friendship and your psychopathy is getting in the way of understanding why, so I will explain it more objectively:

A fake friendship, that you generate for these people, only lasts as long as YOU decide, which means for as long as you are getting what you want. While a real friendship generally does come to and end, it generally does not come to an end because one person no longer is getting some "perk" or benefit. Generally a real friendship lasts despite a persons ability to provide immediate benefits with the implicit understanding that the person will be there for the long term.

Think of what you are doing as collecting insurance premiums. You are collecting regular benefit and the other person thinks they have "long term coverage". Then, when an "accident" happens, think of what you are doing as not paying out. You think that you are providing an equal benefit because you naively think friendship is about a 1-for-1 trade that is settled daily, weekly, or monthly. Your friends/victims are thinking about the friendship as settling on an indefinite time frame with the implied understanding that you will always "pay" your side because the friendship is real. If the friendship is not "real" then a rational person would want a business relationship (a contract) to ensure you "pay" your side.

You are acting like a friend to complete a business deal on friendship terms.
